Nuclear Medicine, Cardiology, Radiation Therapy, IR, Visible Light, and the Ancillary Services

Unit 2: Clinical Engineering. Lesson 10 of 65 in CIIP Academy.

Your PACS holds radiology well. Now cardiology wants echo loops, nuclear medicine wants fused PET and CT, oncology wants radiation therapy plans, and a surgeon wants photos from the operating room. Each is a different kind of object.

Departments and their data

Service              Objects and quirks
Nuclear medicine     256 x 256 matrix at 2 bytes, many frames, small studies
PET                  fused with the CT; both parts must stay matched
Cardiology           echo cine loops, cath angiography, ECG waveforms
Radiation therapy    RT plan, structure set, and dose objects
IR                   fluoroscopy and angiography runs, plus dose report
Visible light        photos and video, often encapsulated or multi-frame

What to remember about each

  • Nuclear medicine and PET: the patient is radioactive after the dose, so timing and handling matter. PET and CT belong to one logical exam.
  • Cardiology: often a separate department system. The cardiology PACS must connect to the enterprise so priors and reports are shared.
  • Radiation therapy: plan, structure set, and dose are special DICOM objects. The oncology system, not only PACS, consumes them. Know the objects at recognition level.
  • IR: procedure room images and dose reports must reach the record.
  • Visible light: captured outside radiology workflows, so the order or patient link is often missing.

Ancillary services

Oncology and tumor tracking across serial exams, surgical planning and orthopedic templating from 3D reconstructions, 3D printing of anatomical models, stereotactic and intraoperative imaging, point-of-care ultrasound and medical image capture, wound care, and digital pathology. Whole-slide pathology images are very large objects, so plan storage and viewing for them separately.

Exam tip: for any non-radiology source, ask three things: how does it get the patient and order link, what object type does it produce, and which system consumes it.
Remember
Nuclear medicine, cardiology, radiation therapy, IR, and visible light each produce their own objects and workflows, and each needs a patient link and a consumer.
Deeper explanation

Nuclear Medicine, Cardiology, Radiation Therapy, IR, Visible Light, and the Ancillary Services, explained slowly

Non-radiology sources and their connections

Each department outside radiology comes with a different object, a different system, and a different gap in the patient link. This table is the map for planning an enterprise connection.

Source               Object type                   Usual system             Usual gap
Nuclear medicine     small multi-frame images      nuclear workstation      PET and CT mismatched
Echo                 cine loops                    cardiology PACS          separate archive and viewer
Cath lab             angiography runs, dose        cardiology PACS          dose report not sent
ECG                  waveform objects              cardiology system        read in separate viewer
Radiation therapy    plan, structure set, dose     oncology system          PACS cannot display them
Endoscopy            video, stills                 visible light capture    no order or patient link
Operating room       photo, video                  capture device           typed patient name
Digital pathology    whole-slide images            pathology system         very large objects

Questions to ask for every source

  1. How does the device learn the patient and the procedure: a worklist, a barcode, or typing?
  2. What object type does it produce, and does the archive accept it?
  3. Which system consumes it, and does the reader need the same patient identity there?
  4. Where does the dose or study record go?

Worked example

A PET and CT exam arrives in PACS as two studies under slightly different patient names. The fusion workstation cannot pair them. The scanner operator typed the name for the PET and used the worklist for the CT. The fix is to correct the PET record with a move or merge under policy and require worklist use for both parts. The prevention is that both parts come from one order.

Radiation therapy at recognition level

A radiation therapy plan holds the beam arrangement. A structure set holds the outlines of the target and organs. A dose object holds the calculated dose distribution. They link to the planning CT by UID. If PACS stores the planning CT but the oncology system holds the plan, the two must reference the same study UID.

Ancillary services

Oncology tumor tracking compares serial exams. Surgical planning and orthopedic templating use 3D reconstructions. 3D printing starts from a segmented volume. Stereotactic and intraoperative systems need fast access to the planning images. Point-of-care ultrasound and medical image capture need a worklist or encounter link. Wound care and digital pathology need storage sized for very large objects.
